fields.Question: The interviewer says: "Design Twitter." and stops talking. How do you run the next 45 minutes?
fields.Answer:
Drive the conversation with a fixed structure so you never stall and never jump straight into boxes.

  • Requirements (5 min): functional (post, follow, home timeline), non-functional (read heavy, timeline latency under ~200 ms, eventual consistency is fine), explicit out of scope (ads, DMs).
  • Estimates (3 min): DAU, QPS for reads and writes, peak factor, storage per year. Only compute what will drive a decision.
  • API and data model (5 min): POST /tweets, GET /timeline?cursor=, tables or key schemas.
  • High level design (10 min): client, LB, stateless services, stores, cache, queue. Walk one read and one write end to end.
  • Deep dives (15 min): the 1 or 2 hard parts (fanout, hot users, storage partitioning). Ask the interviewer which they prefer.
  • Wrap up (5 min): bottlenecks, failure modes, monitoring, what you would do with 10x traffic.

Pitfalls: designing before agreeing scope, spending 15 minutes on estimates, naming technologies without saying why, never stating a tradeoff.
fields.Hint: Requirements, estimates, API, high level, deep dive, wrap up.
fields.Fact: Agree on scope and non-functional requirements first; they decide every later tradeoff.
fields.Source:
System Design Interview: An Insider's Guide, Volume 1 (https://bytebytego.com/)
The System Design Primer (https://github.com/donnemartin/system-design-primer)

fields.Question: Which non-functional requirements should you pin down before designing, and how do they change the design?
fields.Answer:
• Scale: DAU, read to write ratio, peak QPS. Decides caching, sharding, fanout strategy.
  • Latency: p99 target for the hot path. Decides precomputation versus compute on read, CDN, sync versus async.
  • Consistency: can a user see stale data? Read your own writes? Money and inventory need strong consistency; feeds and likes do not.
  • Availability: target (99.9% is ~8.8 h downtime a year, 99.99% is ~53 min). Drives multi AZ or multi region and failover.
  • Durability: can we lose data? Messages and payments no; analytics events maybe.
  • Ordering and exactly once needs: chat ordering per conversation, payment idempotency.

Say them out loud and write them down. Later, justify each decision by pointing back to one of them.
fields.Hint: Scale, latency, consistency, availability, durability.
fields.Fact: Every architecture choice should trace back to a stated requirement.
fields.Source:
System Design Interview: An Insider's Guide, Volume 1 (https://bytebytego.com/)
Site Reliability Engineering: Service Level Objectives (https://sre.google/sre-book/service-level-objectives/)

fields.Question: Estimate: 100 million DAU, each user posts 2 items and reads 50 items a day. What QPS and storage do you plan for?
fields.Answer:
Rule of thumb: a day is ~86,400 s, round to 10^5. So 1 million requests per day is ~12 QPS.

  • Writes: 100M x 2 = 200M/day, about 2,300 QPS average. Peak at 2 to 3x, so plan ~5k to 7k write QPS.
  • Reads: 100M x 50 = 5B/day, about 58k QPS average, ~150k peak. Read to write ratio 25:1, so this is read heavy: cache and precompute.
  • Storage: 200M posts x ~1 KB text and metadata = 200 GB/day, ~73 TB/year before replication (x3 is ~220 TB). Media goes to object storage and is far larger.
  • Bandwidth: 58k reads/s x 1 KB is ~58 MB/s of metadata egress.

Then use the numbers: 150k read QPS is beyond one database, so you need a cache tier and read replicas or a sharded store. State that conclusion; numbers without a conclusion score nothing.
fields.Hint: Divide daily volume by 10^5 to get QPS, multiply by 2 to 3 for peak.
fields.Fact: Estimates exist to justify decisions, so finish each one with what it implies.
fields.Source:
System Design Interview: An Insider's Guide, Volume 1 (https://bytebytego.com/)
The System Design Primer (https://github.com/donnemartin/system-design-primer)

fields.Question: Your design does 6 sequential calls across regions to serve one page. Why is that a problem, and which latency numbers do you reason with?
fields.Answer:
• Main memory reference ~100 ns. SSD random read ~16 to 150 us. Round trip within a datacenter ~0.5 ms. Read 1 MB sequentially from SSD ~1 ms. Disk seek ~10 ms. Cross continent round trip ~150 ms.
  • 6 sequential cross region calls are ~900 ms before any work, which blows a 200 ms budget.

Fixes: keep the request path inside one region, fan out in parallel instead of sequentially, cache or denormalize so one read serves the page, move non critical work to async queues.
fields.Hint: Memory is nanoseconds, datacenter hop is half a millisecond, cross continent is ~150 ms.
fields.Fact: Count network round trips on the critical path; they dominate latency.
fields.Source:
Latency Numbers Every Programmer Should Know (https://gist.github.com/jboner/2841832)
Designing Data-Intensive Applications (https://dataintensive.net/)

fields.Question: You need to serve 150k peak QPS of an API with p50 work of 20 ms per request. How many servers, roughly?
fields.Answer:
Use Little's law: concurrent requests in flight L = arrival rate x latency = 150,000 x 0.02 s = 3,000 concurrent requests.

  • If one server comfortably handles ~200 concurrent requests (for example 32 cores with mostly I/O bound work and a thread pool or async runtime), you need ~15 servers.
  • Add headroom so you run at ~50 to 60% utilization and can lose an AZ: ~30 to 40 servers across 3 AZs.
  • Queueing delay grows sharply as utilization approaches 100%, which is why headroom matters for p99.

Say the assumption about per server capacity explicitly; the interviewer cares about the method, not the exact constant.
fields.Hint: L = lambda x W.
fields.Fact: Little's law turns throughput and latency into concurrency, which sizes pools and fleets.
fields.Source:
A Proof for the Queuing Formula: L = lambda W (https://doi.org/10.1287/opre.9.3.383)
Site Reliability Engineering: Handling Overload (https://sre.google/sre-book/handling-overload/)

fields.Question: For each feature, would you choose strong or eventual consistency, and why: like counts, account balance, username uniqueness, home feed, inventory at checkout?
fields.Answer:
• Like counts: eventual. Being off by a few for seconds is invisible; use async or sharded counters.
  • Account balance: strong. Every debit must see the latest value or you allow double spend. Single leader with transactions, or a ledger with serializable checks.
  • Username uniqueness: strong for the claim step: a unique constraint on one leader, or a conditional write (compare and set) on the key.
  • Home feed: eventual. A post appearing 2 s late is fine; add read your own writes so the author sees their own post immediately.
  • Inventory at checkout: strong for the decrement (UPDATE ... SET stock = stock - 1 WHERE id = ? AND stock > 0), eventual for the displayed "only 3 left".

Framing: under a partition you pick consistency or availability (CAP); with no partition you still trade latency for consistency (PACELC). Pick per operation, not per system.
fields.Hint: Would a stale read cost money or break an invariant?
fields.Fact: Choose consistency per operation: strong where an invariant or money is at stake, eventual elsewhere.
fields.Source:
Designing Data-Intensive Applications (https://dataintensive.net/)
Brewer's Conjecture and the Feasibility of Consistent, Available, Partition-Tolerant Web Services (https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/564585.564601)
Consistency Tradeoffs in Modern Distributed Database System Design (https://www.cs.umd.edu/~abadi/papers/abadi-pacelc.pdf)

fields.Question: Users edit their profile, refresh, and see the old version. Reads go to async replicas. How do you fix it without sending all reads to the leader?
fields.Answer:
Cause: replication lag breaks read your own writes.

  • Route reads of data the user can edit (their own profile) to the leader; everything else to replicas.
  • Or remember the time (or log position) of the user's last write, and for the next N seconds read from the leader or only from replicas caught up past that position.
  • Or have the client send its last write version; the server waits for or picks a replica at least that fresh.
  • Across devices, store the last write position server side, not in a client cookie.

Related anomalies to mention: monotonic reads (pin a user to one replica so time does not go backwards) and consistent prefix reads (causally related writes in the same partition).
fields.Hint: Track the user's last write position.
fields.Fact: Read your own writes is a per user guarantee; you only pay leader reads for recently written data.
fields.Source: Designing Data-Intensive Applications (https://dataintensive.net/)

fields.Question: Your single Postgres is at capacity on writes. How do you choose a partitioning (sharding) scheme, and what goes wrong?
fields.Answer:
• Pick the shard key from the access pattern: the key most queries filter by (user_id for a social app, tenant_id for SaaS), so most requests hit one shard.
  • Hash partitioning: even load, but range scans across keys hit every shard.
  • Range partitioning: efficient range scans, but sequential keys (timestamps, auto increment ids) create a hot shard.
  • Consistent hashing or many virtual partitions (for example 1024 logical shards mapped to N machines) so adding a node moves a small fraction of data instead of rehashing everything.

Pitfalls: hot keys (a celebrity) still overload one shard: split the key with a suffix or cache it. Cross shard joins and transactions become application work or sagas. Secondary indexes are either local (scatter gather reads) or global (async, eventually consistent). Resharding needs dual writes or a directory service.

Before sharding, mention cheaper steps: read replicas, caching, vertical scaling, archiving cold data.
fields.Hint: Shard by the key most queries filter on.
fields.Fact: A good shard key keeps the common query on one shard and spreads writes evenly.
fields.Source:
Designing Data-Intensive Applications (https://dataintensive.net/)
Sharding pattern (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/patterns/sharding)
Consistent Hashing and Random Trees (https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/258533.258660)

fields.Question: Compare single leader, multi leader and leaderless replication. When would you pick each in an interview design?
fields.Answer:
• Single leader: all writes to one node, replicas follow. Simple, supports transactions and strong reads from the leader. Failover can lose unreplicated writes if async. Default choice for OLTP (users, orders, payments).
  • Multi leader: one leader per region, writes accepted locally, replicated async. Low write latency across regions and offline clients, but you need conflict resolution (last write wins loses data; CRDTs or app merge). Collaborative editing, multi region active active.
  • Leaderless (Dynamo style): write to N replicas, succeed on W acks, read R replicas; if R + W > N reads overlap the latest write. High availability, tunable consistency, read repair and hinted handoff. Shopping carts, KV stores, time series.

Follow ups: sync versus async replication (durability versus latency), split brain on failover (use fencing tokens or consensus for leader election), replication lag anomalies.
fields.Hint: Where are writes accepted, and who resolves conflicts?
fields.Fact: Single leader is the default; reach for multi leader or leaderless only for multi region writes or extreme availability.
fields.Source:
Designing Data-Intensive Applications (https://dataintensive.net/)
Dynamo: Amazon's Highly Available Key-value Store (https://www.allthingsdistributed.com/files/amazon-dynamo-sosp2007.pdf)
In Search of an Understandable Consensus Algorithm (https://raft.github.io/raft.pdf)

fields.Question: You add Redis in front of a database for product pages. Which caching pattern do you use, and how do you keep it from serving stale or broken data?
fields.Answer:
Default: cache aside. Read: get from cache, on miss read the DB and set with a TTL. Write: update the DB, then delete the cache key (delete, not set, to avoid racing writers installing an old value).

  • Write through: write cache and DB together; cache always warm, writes slower, caches data nobody reads.
  • Write behind: write cache, flush to DB async; fast writes, risk of loss on cache failure.
  • Read through: the cache library loads on miss; same semantics as cache aside, less app code.

Pitfalls and fixes

  • Stale data: TTL as a safety net plus invalidation on write; for stricter needs, version keys or CDC driven invalidation.
  • Thundering herd on a hot key expiry: single flight or lease so one request recomputes, others wait or get stale value.
  • Cache penetration (lookups for keys that do not exist): cache negative results briefly or use a Bloom filter.
  • Avalanche (many keys expire together): add random jitter to TTLs.
  • Cache down: the DB must survive the miss storm, or shed load.
fields.Hint: Cache aside: on write, update DB then delete the key.
fields.Fact: Delete on write plus TTL is the simplest cache invalidation that stays correct under races in practice.
fields.Source:
Cache-Aside pattern (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/patterns/cache-aside)
Scaling Memcache at Facebook (https://www.usenix.org/conference/nsdi13/technical-sessions/presentation/nishtala)
Redis: Key eviction (https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/reference/eviction/)

fields.Question: When do you put a message queue between two services, and what delivery guarantees do you design for?
fields.Answer:
• Use a queue to absorb bursts, decouple availability (producer keeps working if consumer is down), fan out one event to many consumers, and move slow work off the request path.
  • Assume at least once delivery: consumers crash after processing but before acking, so messages are redelivered. Make consumers idempotent (dedupe by message id or use idempotent writes).
  • Exactly once end to end is really at least once plus idempotency, or a transactional system like Kafka transactions within Kafka.
  • Ordering: only guaranteed per partition (Kafka) or per message group (SQS FIFO). Partition by the entity that needs ordering (conversation_id, account_id).
  • Poison messages: retry with backoff, then move to a dead letter queue and alert.
  • Backpressure: monitor consumer lag; scale consumers up to the partition count.

Log versus queue: Kafka keeps a replayable log with consumer offsets (good for event sourcing and multiple readers); SQS or RabbitMQ delete on ack (good for task distribution).
fields.Hint: At least once delivery plus idempotent consumers.
fields.Fact: Design every consumer to tolerate duplicates; ordering only exists within a partition.
fields.Source:
Apache Kafka Documentation (https://kafka.apache.org/documentation/)
Amazon SQS Developer Guide (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/welcome.html)
Designing Data-Intensive Applications (https://dataintensive.net/)

fields.Question: A client times out calling POST /payments and retries. How do you guarantee the customer is charged once?
fields.Answer:
Idempotency key: the client generates a unique key (UUID) per logical operation and sends it on every retry.

  • Server stores (key, request_hash, status, response) with a unique constraint on key, in the same transaction as the side effect where possible.
  • First request inserts the key as in progress, does the work, saves the response. A retry with the same key returns the saved response.
  • A concurrent retry while the first is in progress gets 409 or waits; it must not run the work again.
  • Same key with a different request body is a client bug: reject with 4xx.
  • Expire keys after a window (Stripe keeps them 24 hours).
def create_payment(key, body):
    with db.transaction():
        row = db.get_for_update("idem", key)
        if row:
            if row.request_hash != hash(body):
                raise Conflict("key reused with different body")
            return row.response
        db.insert("idem", key=key, request_hash=hash(body), status="started")
    response = charge_provider(body, idempotency_key=key)
    db.update("idem", key, status="done", response=response)
    return response

Pitfall: the downstream provider must also be called idempotently (pass the key through), otherwise a crash between charge and save still double charges.
fields.Hint: Client generated key, stored server side with a unique constraint.
fields.Fact: Retries are safe only when every hop dedupes on the same idempotency key.
fields.Source:
Stripe API: Idempotent requests (https://docs.stripe.com/api/idempotent_requests)
Designing robust and predictable APIs with idempotency (https://stripe.com/blog/idempotency)

fields.Question: Your order service writes to its database and then publishes OrderCreated to Kafka. Sometimes the event is lost, sometimes it is sent for an order that rolled back. Fix it.
fields.Answer:
Problem: a dual write to two systems cannot be atomic.

Transactional outbox: in the same DB transaction as the order insert, insert a row into an outbox table. A relay process (poller or CDC such as Debezium reading the WAL) publishes outbox rows to Kafka and marks them sent.

  • Atomic: the event exists if and only if the order committed.
  • Delivery is at least once (relay can crash after publish, before marking), so consumers dedupe by event id.
  • Ordering per aggregate is preserved if the relay publishes in commit order and keys messages by order_id.

Alternatives: event sourcing (the event log is the source of truth), or CDC directly on the business table. Avoid 2PC across DB and broker in interviews; it couples availability.
fields.Hint: Write the event into the same database transaction.
fields.Fact: Never dual write; commit the event with the data and relay it asynchronously.
fields.Source:
Pattern: Transactional outbox (https://microservices.io/patterns/data/transactional-outbox.html)
Designing Data-Intensive Applications (https://dataintensive.net/)

fields.Question: Booking a trip reserves a flight, a hotel and charges a card, each in a different service. How do you keep it consistent without a distributed transaction?
fields.Answer:
Saga: a sequence of local transactions, each with a compensating action that semantically undoes it.

  • Steps: reserve flight, reserve hotel, charge card. If charge fails, run cancel hotel then cancel flight.
  • Orchestration: a coordinator (state machine, workflow engine like Temporal or Step Functions) calls each step and drives compensation. Easier to reason about and monitor.
  • Choreography: each service reacts to events. Fewer central pieces but hard to follow with many steps.
  • Every step and compensation must be idempotent and retryable; persist saga state.
  • Order steps so the hardest to compensate (charging money, sending email) go last, and use reservations with expiry (hold, then confirm).

Tradeoff: no isolation. Other requests can see intermediate state (hotel held, card not charged). Mitigate with pending states and semantic locks.
fields.Hint: Local transactions plus compensating actions.
fields.Fact: Sagas trade isolation for availability; put irreversible steps last.
fields.Source:
Saga distributed transactions pattern (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/patterns/saga)
Designing Data-Intensive Applications (https://dataintensive.net/)

fields.Question: A dependency starts failing and your service retries every failed call 3 times immediately. The outage gets worse. Why, and what should the retry policy be?
fields.Answer:
Why: immediate retries multiply load on a struggling service (3 retries at each of 3 layers is up to 64x), synchronized clients retry in waves, and the dependency never recovers.

  • Retry only idempotent or idempotency keyed operations, and only retryable errors (timeouts, 503, 429), never 400s.
  • Exponential backoff with full jitter: sleep a random time in [0, min(cap, base x 2^attempt)].
  • Cap attempts and use a retry budget (for example retries at most 10% of requests) per client.
  • Retry at one layer only, usually closest to the user.
  • Add a circuit breaker: after a failure threshold, fail fast for a cool down, then let a few trial requests through (half open).
  • Respect Retry-After headers and propagate deadlines so callers stop work whose caller already gave up.
import random, time

def call_with_retry(fn, attempts=5, base=0.1, cap=5.0):
    for attempt in range(attempts):
        try:
            return fn()
        except RetryableError:
            if attempt == attempts - 1:
                raise
            time.sleep(random.uniform(0, min(cap, base * 2 ** attempt)))
fields.Hint: Backoff, jitter, budget, circuit breaker.
fields.Fact: Uncontrolled retries turn a partial outage into a cascading failure.
fields.Source:
Exponential Backoff And Jitter (https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/architecture/exponential-backoff-and-jitter/)
CircuitBreaker (https://martinfowler.com/bliki/CircuitBreaker.html)
Site Reliability Engineering: Addressing Cascading Failures (https://sre.google/sre-book/addressing-cascading-failures/)

fields.Question: Design a service that generates unique 64 bit IDs at 100k per second across many machines, roughly sortable by time, with no central coordination per ID.
fields.Answer:
Snowflake layout: 1 sign bit, 41 bits of milliseconds since a custom epoch (~69 years), 10 bits machine id (1024 workers), 12 bits sequence (4096 IDs per ms per worker).

import threading, time

class Snowflake:
    EPOCH = 1_700_000_000_000

    def __init__(self, worker_id):
        assert 0 <= worker_id < 1024
        self.worker_id = worker_id
        self.last_ms = -1
        self.seq = 0
        self.lock = threading.Lock()

    def next_id(self):
        with self.lock:
            now = int(time.time() * 1000)
            if now < self.last_ms:
                raise RuntimeError("clock moved backwards")
            if now == self.last_ms:
                self.seq = (self.seq + 1) & 0xFFF
                if self.seq == 0:
                    while now <= self.last_ms:
                        now = int(time.time() * 1000)
            else:
                self.seq = 0
            self.last_ms = now
            return ((now - self.EPOCH) << 22) | (self.worker_id << 12) | self.seq
  • Worker ids are assigned once at startup (config, ZooKeeper or etcd lease), not per ID.
  • Clock skew: refuse or wait when the clock goes backwards; use NTP with slew, not step.
  • Alternatives: DB auto increment (single point, not scalable), ticket server ranges (batches of IDs per node), UUIDv4 (128 bits, not sortable), UUIDv7 or ULID (time ordered, 128 bits).

Complexity: O(1) per ID, no network calls.
fields.Hint: Timestamp, machine id, sequence.
fields.Fact: Time prefixed IDs give rough ordering and index locality without coordination.
fields.Source:
Announcing Snowflake (https://blog.x.com/engineering/en_us/a/2010/announcing-snowflake)
System Design Interview: An Insider's Guide, Volume 1 (https://bytebytego.com/)

fields.Question: One key (a celebrity's profile, a flash sale item) receives 500k reads per second and melts its cache shard. What do you do?
fields.Answer:
• Detect hot keys with per key sampling or top k counters on the cache proxies.
  • Local in process cache on app servers with a short TTL (1 to 5 s): absorbs most reads with no network hop.
  • Replicate the hot key: store it as key#0..key#N on different shards and read a random copy; writes update all copies.
  • Request coalescing: collapse concurrent misses into one backend fetch.
  • CDN if the content is public.

For hot write keys (like counter on a viral post): shard the counter into N sub counters and sum on read, or buffer increments and flush in batches.

Tradeoff: more staleness and more write fanout in exchange for spreading load.
fields.Hint: Spread one key across many copies or cache it closer to the caller.
fields.Fact: Partitioning cannot fix a single hot key; you must replicate or cache it.
fields.Source:
Scaling Memcache at Facebook (https://www.usenix.org/conference/nsdi13/technical-sessions/presentation/nishtala)
Designing Data-Intensive Applications (https://dataintensive.net/)

fields.Question: Traffic suddenly doubles beyond capacity. How should the system degrade instead of falling over?
fields.Answer:
• Load shedding: reject excess work early (at the LB or the first service) with 503 or 429 when queue length or concurrency exceeds a limit, rather than letting latency grow for everyone.
  • Prioritize: keep checkout and login, shed recommendations and analytics. Tag requests with criticality.
  • Bounded queues and timeouts everywhere; an unbounded queue is just slow failure.
  • Graceful degradation: serve cached or simplified responses (stale feed, no personalization).
  • Deadline propagation: do not process requests whose client already timed out.
  • Autoscale, but it lags by minutes, so shedding covers the gap.
  • Rate limit per client so one abusive caller cannot consume the capacity.

Pitfall: health checks that fail under load cause the LB to remove servers, concentrating load and cascading. Keep health checks cheap and separate from overload.
fields.Hint: Fail some requests fast so the rest succeed.
fields.Fact: Under overload, rejecting early is cheaper than serving everything slowly.
fields.Source:
Site Reliability Engineering: Handling Overload (https://sre.google/sre-book/handling-overload/)
Site Reliability Engineering: Addressing Cascading Failures (https://sre.google/sre-book/addressing-cascading-failures/)

fields.Question: The interviewer asks: "Why did you pick a relational database here and not Cassandra?" How do you answer for an e-commerce orders service versus a chat message store?
fields.Answer:
• Orders: relational. Multi row transactions (order, items, payment status), constraints, ad hoc queries for support and finance, moderate write volume that a sharded or well provisioned Postgres or MySQL handles.
  • Chat messages: wide column (Cassandra, ScyllaDB, HBase). Huge append heavy write volume, access is always by conversation and time range, which maps to partition key conversation_id (often bucketed by time) and clustering key message_id. No joins or cross row transactions needed.

How to argue: start from access patterns, consistency needs, and scale. Relational: flexible queries and transactions. Wide column or KV: predictable key based access at massive write scale, tunable consistency, you design tables per query. Document stores: self contained aggregates with flexible schema.

Pitfall: choosing NoSQL for "scale" without saying what query it serves, or ignoring that you lose joins and transactions.
fields.Hint: Access pattern and transaction needs decide the store.
fields.Fact: Pick storage from the queries you must serve and the invariants you must protect.
fields.Source:
Designing Data-Intensive Applications (https://dataintensive.net/)
How Discord Stores Trillions of Messages (https://discord.com/blog/how-discord-stores-trillions-of-messages)
Bigtable: A Distributed Storage System for Structured Data (https://research.google/pubs/bigtable-a-distributed-storage-system-for-structured-data/)

fields.Question: Two workers must never process the same job at the same time. Someone proposes a Redis lock with SETNX and a TTL. Is that safe?
fields.Answer:
Not on its own. A worker can pause (GC, network stall) past the TTL; the lock expires, a second worker takes it, and the first wakes up still believing it holds the lock.

  • Fencing tokens: the lock service returns a monotonically increasing token; the protected resource (DB, storage) rejects writes with a token lower than the highest it has seen.
  • Use a consensus backed lock service (etcd, ZooKeeper) for correctness critical locks; Redis locks are fine for efficiency (avoiding duplicate work) when occasional overlap is harmless.
  • Better still, avoid locks: make the operation idempotent, or use a conditional write (UPDATE jobs SET owner = ? WHERE id = ? AND owner IS NULL), or a queue with visibility timeouts.

Follow up: release the lock only if you still own it (compare the stored value before delete, atomically via a Lua script).
fields.Hint: Leases expire while the holder is paused.
fields.Fact: A lock is only safe if the resource itself checks a fencing token.
fields.Source:
How to do distributed locking (https://martin.kleppmann.com/2016/02/08/how-to-do-distributed-locking.html)
Designing Data-Intensive Applications (https://dataintensive.net/)

fields.Question: Two concurrent requests both check "is the doctor on call count at least 2?", both see 2, and each takes one doctor off call, leaving zero. What went wrong and how do you prevent it?
fields.Answer:
Write skew: each transaction reads the same set, then writes different rows, so row level locks or snapshot isolation do not detect a conflict.

  • Use SERIALIZABLE isolation (Postgres SSI detects this and aborts one transaction; retry it).
  • Or lock the rows you read: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE on the on call rows.
  • Or materialize the conflict: a single row (shift counter) both transactions must update, so they conflict on it.
  • Or enforce with a constraint where possible.

Related anomalies: lost update (read modify write; fix with atomic UPDATE x = x + 1 or compare and set), phantom reads (range predicates; fix with serializable or predicate or index range locks).
fields.Hint: Snapshot isolation does not prevent write skew.
fields.Fact: When an invariant spans several rows, use serializable isolation or lock the rows you read.
fields.Source:
PostgreSQL: Transaction Isolation (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/transaction-iso.html)
Designing Data-Intensive Applications (https://dataintensive.net/)
Jepsen: Consistency Models (https://jepsen.io/consistency)

fields.Question: Design a URL shortener like bit.ly: 100M new URLs per month, 10:1 read to write ratio, links live for years.
fields.Answer:
Requirements: shorten, redirect, optional custom alias and expiry. Redirect must be fast and highly available; analytics can be async.

Estimates: 100M/month is ~40 writes/s, ~400 reads/s average, a few thousand at peak. 100M x 12 x 10 years = 12B URLs x ~500 bytes is ~6 TB. Small; storage is not the hard part.

  • API: POST /urls {long_url, alias?, expires_at?} returns short code; GET /{code} returns 301 or 302 with Location.
  • Key generation: base62 of a unique 64 bit id (from a counter range per server or Snowflake). 7 base62 chars give 62^7, ~3.5 trillion codes.
  • Storage: KV or sharded table code -> long_url, created_at, expires_at, owner. Shard by code.
  • Read path: LB, stateless redirect service, cache (Redis) in front of the store; hot links are heavily skewed so the hit rate is high. CDN or edge can serve redirects too.
  • Analytics: emit click events to a queue, aggregate offline. Never block the redirect on analytics.

Deep dive tradeoffs: 301 is cached by browsers (less load, lose click counts), 302 keeps every click visible. Hashing the long URL (MD5, take 7 chars) needs collision checks; counter based ids do not but are guessable (shuffle bits or add a random component if enumeration matters). Dedup of identical long URLs is optional and costs an extra index.
fields.Hint: Unique id to base62, cache in front of a KV store.
fields.Fact: The core problem is collision free short key generation; reads are a cached key lookup.

fields.Question: Coding: implement encode and decode between a non negative integer id and a base62 short code.
fields.Answer:
ALPHABET = "0123456789abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyzABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ"
INDEX = {c: i for i, c in enumerate(ALPHABET)}

def encode(n: int) -> str:
    if n == 0:
        return ALPHABET[0]
    out = []
    while n:
        n, r = divmod(n, 62)
        out.append(ALPHABET[r])
    return "".join(reversed(out))

def decode(s: str) -> int:
    n = 0
    for c in s:
        n = n * 62 + INDEX[c]
    return n

Complexity: O(log62 n) time and space, at most 11 characters for a 64 bit id.

Follow ups: fixed length codes (left pad), avoiding ambiguous characters (drop 0, O, l, I and use base58), making sequential ids non guessable (apply a reversible bijection such as multiplying by an odd constant mod 2^k, or a small Feistel cipher, before encoding).
fields.Hint: Repeated divmod by 62.
fields.Fact: Base62 encoding is just positional number conversion.
fields.Source: System Design Interview: An Insider's Guide, Volume 1 (https://bytebytego.com/)

fields.Question: In your URL shortener, how do multiple app servers generate unique short codes without hitting a single counter on every request?
fields.Answer:
• Range allocation: a coordinator (a DB row or ZooKeeper or etcd) hands each server a block of 1M ids; the server increments locally and base62 encodes. A crash wastes at most one block, which is fine.
  • Snowflake style ids: timestamp plus worker id plus sequence, no coordination per id; codes are slightly longer.
  • Pre generated key service: generate random codes offline into an unused table; servers claim batches. Random, unguessable, but more moving parts.
  • Hash of URL: take the first 7 base62 chars of a hash; on collision append a salt and retry. Needs a uniqueness check on every write (conditional insert).

Recommendation: range allocation for simplicity, plus a bijective scramble if codes should not be enumerable. Custom aliases go through a conditional insert that fails if the code exists.
fields.Hint: Lease blocks of ids to each server.
fields.Fact: Batching id allocation removes the coordinator from the hot path.
fields.Source:
System Design Interview: An Insider's Guide, Volume 1 (https://bytebytego.com/)
Announcing Snowflake (https://blog.x.com/engineering/en_us/a/2010/announcing-snowflake)

fields.Question: Design a distributed rate limiter for a public API: 100 requests per minute per API key, enforced across 50 gateway servers.
fields.Answer:
• Where: in the API gateway or a sidecar, before any business logic. Return 429 with Retry-After and X-RateLimit-Remaining headers.
  • Algorithm: token bucket (allows short bursts, smooth refill) or sliding window counter (approximation weighting the previous window). Fixed window is simplest but allows 2x bursts at window edges.
  • Shared state: Redis keyed by rl:{api_key}. Do the read and update atomically in a Lua script (or INCR plus EXPIRE for fixed window) to avoid races between gateways.
  • Rules: stored in config, cached on gateways; different limits per plan, endpoint, IP.

Deep dives

  • Latency: one Redis round trip (~0.5 ms) per request. To cut it, keep local counters and sync to Redis every few hundred ms; accept slight over admission.
  • Redis failure: fail open (allow traffic) for availability, or fail closed for abuse sensitive endpoints. Say which and why.
  • Multi region: per region limits, or async global sync with approximate counts.
  • Hot keys: shard Redis by key; a single key lives on one shard.

Complexity: O(1) per request and O(1) memory per key for token bucket or sliding window counter; sliding window log is O(limit) memory per key.
fields.Hint: Token bucket in Redis with an atomic script.
fields.Fact: A distributed limiter is an atomic counter per key in shared fast storage, with an explicit fail open or fail closed choice.
fields.Source:

fields.Question: Coding: implement a token bucket rate limiter with capacity C tokens and a refill rate of R tokens per second. allow() returns True if a request may proceed.
fields.Answer:
import time

class TokenBucket:
    def __init__(self, capacity: float, rate: float):
        self.capacity = capacity
        self.rate = rate
        self.tokens = capacity
        self.updated = time.monotonic()

    def allow(self, cost: float = 1) -> bool:
        now = time.monotonic()
        elapsed = now - self.updated
        self.tokens = min(self.capacity, self.tokens + elapsed * self.rate)
        self.updated = now
        if self.tokens >= cost:
            self.tokens -= cost
            return True
        return False
  • Lazy refill: compute tokens from elapsed time instead of a background timer.
  • Use a monotonic clock so wall clock jumps do not mint tokens.
  • O(1) time and memory per key. Store (tokens, updated) per key in a dict, or in a Redis hash updated by a Lua script for a distributed version.
  • Thread safety: wrap allow in a lock, or shard keys across locks.

Follow up: leaky bucket is the same idea but outputs at a constant rate (a queue drained at R per second), smoothing bursts instead of allowing them.
fields.Hint: Refill lazily from elapsed time.
fields.Fact: Token bucket allows bursts up to capacity while bounding the long term rate.
fields.Source:
System Design Interview: An Insider's Guide, Volume 1 (https://bytebytego.com/)
Scaling your API with rate limiters (https://stripe.com/blog/rate-limiters)

fields.Question: Coding: implement a sliding window rate limiter that allows at most N requests per client in any rolling 60 second window. Then explain how to make it O(1) memory.
fields.Answer:
import time
from collections import defaultdict, deque

class SlidingWindowLog:
    def __init__(self, limit: int, window: float = 60.0):
        self.limit = limit
        self.window = window
        self.log = defaultdict(deque)

    def allow(self, client: str) -> bool:
        now = time.monotonic()
        q = self.log[client]
        while q and q[0] <= now - self.window:
            q.popleft()
        if len(q) < self.limit:
            q.append(now)
            return True
        return False

Complexity: amortized O(1) time, O(N) memory per client. Exact.

O(1) memory: sliding window counter. Keep counts for the current and previous fixed windows. Estimated count = current + previous x (1 - elapsed_fraction_of_current_window). Allow if the estimate is below N. Cloudflare reported this approximation is very close to exact for real traffic.

Distributed: in Redis use a sorted set per client (ZREMRANGEBYSCORE, ZCARD, ZADD in one Lua script) for the log, or two INCR counters with TTL for the counter version.
fields.Hint: Deque of timestamps; evict older than the window.
fields.Fact: The log is exact but costs memory per request; the weighted two window counter is O(1) and close enough.
fields.Source:
How we built rate limiting capable of scaling to millions of domains (https://blog.cloudflare.com/counting-things-a-lot-of-different-things/)

fields.Question: Design a distributed key value store (like Dynamo or Cassandra) that stays available for writes during node failures and network partitions.
fields.Answer:
• Partitioning: consistent hashing with virtual nodes; each key is owned by the next N distinct nodes on the ring (its preference list).
  • Replication and quorums: N = 3. Write succeeds after W acks, read queries R replicas. R + W > N (for example 2 and 2) gives overlapping quorums; W = 1 favors write availability.
  • Failures: sloppy quorum with hinted handoff (a neighbor accepts writes for a down node and forwards later). Read repair fixes stale replicas on read; anti entropy with Merkle trees fixes the rest in the background.
  • Conflicts: concurrent writes produce siblings. Resolve with last write wins (simple, loses data) or vector clocks plus client merge (Dynamo carts), or CRDTs.
  • Membership: gossip protocol for ring state and failure detection.
  • Storage engine per node: LSM tree: write ahead log, memtable, flushed to immutable SSTables, compaction, Bloom filters to skip SSTables on reads.

Tradeoffs: this is AP under CAP. If the interviewer wants strong consistency, switch to per partition consensus (Raft groups, like etcd, TiKV or CockroachDB) and accept unavailability of a partition without a majority.
fields.Hint: Consistent hashing, quorums, hinted handoff, LSM.
fields.Fact: Leaderless replication with quorums trades consistency for write availability; consensus per partition trades the other way.
fields.Source:
Dynamo: Amazon's Highly Available Key-value Store (https://www.allthingsdistributed.com/files/amazon-dynamo-sosp2007.pdf)
Designing Data-Intensive Applications (https://dataintensive.net/)
The Log-Structured Merge-Tree (LSM-Tree) (https://www.cs.umb.edu/~poneil/lsmtree.pdf)
In Search of an Understandable Consensus Algorithm (https://raft.github.io/raft.pdf)

fields.Question: Coding: implement a consistent hash ring with virtual nodes: add_node, remove_node, and get_node(key).
fields.Answer:
import bisect, hashlib

def h(s: str) -> int:
    return int.from_bytes(hashlib.md5(s.encode()).digest()[:8], "big")

class HashRing:
    def __init__(self, vnodes: int = 100):
        self.vnodes = vnodes
        self.hashes = []
        self.owner = {}

    def add_node(self, node: str):
        for i in range(self.vnodes):
            k = h(f"{node}#{i}")
            bisect.insort(self.hashes, k)
            self.owner[k] = node

    def remove_node(self, node: str):
        for i in range(self.vnodes):
            k = h(f"{node}#{i}")
            self.hashes.pop(bisect.bisect_left(self.hashes, k))
            del self.owner[k]

    def get_node(self, key: str) -> str:
        if not self.hashes:
            raise KeyError("empty ring")
        i = bisect.bisect_right(self.hashes, h(key)) % len(self.hashes)
        return self.owner[self.hashes[i]]
  • Lookup O(log V) with V total virtual nodes. Adding a node is O(V log V) here due to list inserts; fine for rare membership changes.
  • Adding or removing a node moves only ~1/N of keys, versus nearly all keys with hash(key) % N.
  • Virtual nodes smooth out load and let bigger machines take more vnodes.
  • Replication: walk clockwise to collect the next R distinct physical nodes.

Alternatives: rendezvous (highest random weight) hashing, jump consistent hash for numbered buckets.
fields.Hint: Sorted ring of hashes, binary search clockwise.
fields.Fact: Consistent hashing bounds data movement on membership change to about 1/N of keys.
fields.Source:
Consistent Hashing and Random Trees (https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/258533.258660)
Dynamo: Amazon's Highly Available Key-value Store (https://www.allthingsdistributed.com/files/amazon-dynamo-sosp2007.pdf)

fields.Question: Your KV store node must sustain very high write throughput on SSDs. Walk through the write path and read path of an LSM tree, and its tradeoffs versus a B tree.
fields.Answer:
• Write: append to write ahead log (durability), insert into in memory sorted memtable, acknowledge. When the memtable is full, flush it as an immutable sorted SSTable. Sequential writes only.
  • Read: check memtable, then SSTables newest to oldest. A Bloom filter per SSTable skips files that cannot contain the key; a sparse index finds the block.
  • Compaction: merge SSTables in the background, dropping overwritten values and tombstones. Size tiered (write friendly) or leveled (read and space friendly).
  • Deletes: write a tombstone; data disappears after compaction.

Versus B tree: LSM has higher write throughput and better compression but read amplification and compaction spikes; B tree updates pages in place, gives predictable reads and easy range scans, but random writes and write amplification from page splits. Choose LSM for write heavy (logs, messages, time series), B tree for read heavy OLTP.
fields.Hint: WAL, memtable, SSTables, compaction.
fields.Fact: LSM trees turn random writes into sequential ones at the cost of read and compaction work.
fields.Source:
The Log-Structured Merge-Tree (LSM-Tree) (https://www.cs.umb.edu/~poneil/lsmtree.pdf)
Bigtable: A Distributed Storage System for Structured Data (https://research.google/pubs/bigtable-a-distributed-storage-system-for-structured-data/)
Designing Data-Intensive Applications (https://dataintensive.net/)

fields.Question: Design a distributed in memory cache (like Memcached or Redis Cluster) serving 1M reads per second with sub millisecond latency.
fields.Answer:
• Partitioning: consistent hashing (client side or via a proxy like mcrouter or twemproxy) or fixed hash slots (Redis Cluster uses 16,384 slots mapped to nodes).
  • Node internals: hash table plus LRU (or LFU) eviction, slab allocation to limit fragmentation, TTL per entry with lazy plus periodic expiry.
  • Replication: primary with replicas per shard for availability; async, so a failover can lose recent writes. Fine for a cache, the DB is the source of truth.
  • Sizing: working set, not total data. If 20% of keys serve 80% of reads, cache that 20% plus headroom.
  • Client behavior: connection pooling, pipelining or multi get, short timeouts, treat cache errors as misses.

Deep dive problems: thundering herd on popular key expiry (leases or single flight), hot keys (local L1 cache, key replication), node failure causing a miss storm on the DB (gutter pool or replicas), cross region invalidation (invalidate from the DB commit log).

Consistency: cache aside with delete on write; Facebook uses leases to stop stale sets after a concurrent delete.
fields.Hint: Consistent hashing, LRU per node, replicas per shard.
fields.Fact: A cache cluster is sharded hash tables; the hard parts are herds, hot keys and invalidation.
fields.Source:
Scaling Memcache at Facebook (https://www.usenix.org/conference/nsdi13/technical-sessions/presentation/nishtala)
Redis: Key eviction (https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/reference/eviction/)
Cache-Aside pattern (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/patterns/cache-aside)

fields.Question: Coding: implement an LRU cache with get(key) and put(key, value), both O(1), with a fixed capacity.
fields.Answer:
from collections import OrderedDict

class LRUCache:
    def __init__(self, capacity: int):
        self.capacity = capacity
        self.data = OrderedDict()

    def get(self, key):
        if key not in self.data:
            return None
        self.data.move_to_end(key)
        return self.data[key]

    def put(self, key, value):
        if key in self.data:
            self.data.move_to_end(key)
        self.data[key] = value
        if len(self.data) > self.capacity:
            self.data.popitem(last=False)

Without OrderedDict (often required): a hash map from key to node plus a doubly linked list with sentinel head and tail. get moves the node to the front; put inserts at the front and evicts from the tail. Every operation is pointer surgery, O(1).

  • Space O(capacity).
  • Thread safety: one lock, or shard into N independent LRUs by key hash.
  • Follow ups: TTL per entry (store expiry, check on get), LFU (frequency buckets of linked lists, O(1)), approximate LRU like Redis (sample a few keys, evict the oldest).
fields.Hint: Hash map plus doubly linked list.
fields.Fact: O(1) LRU needs a map for lookup and a linked list for recency order.
fields.Source:
Python documentation: collections.OrderedDict (https://docs.python.org/3/library/collections.html#collections.OrderedDict)
Redis: Key eviction (https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/reference/eviction/)

fields.Question: Coding: implement an in memory key value store with set(key, value, ttl_seconds), get(key), and memory that does not grow forever with expired keys.
fields.Answer:
import heapq, time

class TTLStore:
    def __init__(self):
        self.data = {}
        self.expiries = []

    def set(self, key, value, ttl):
        expires_at = time.monotonic() + ttl
        self.data[key] = (value, expires_at)
        heapq.heappush(self.expiries, (expires_at, key))
        self._purge()

    def get(self, key):
        item = self.data.get(key)
        if item is None:
            return None
        value, expires_at = item
        if expires_at <= time.monotonic():
            del self.data[key]
            return None
        return value

    def _purge(self):
        now = time.monotonic()
        while self.expiries and self.expiries[0][0] <= now:
            expires_at, key = heapq.heappop(self.expiries)
            item = self.data.get(key)
            if item and item[1] == expires_at:
                del self.data[key]
  • Lazy expiry on get guarantees correctness; the min heap purge reclaims memory.
  • The heap can hold stale entries for overwritten keys; the item[1] == expires_at check skips them.
  • set is O(log n) amortized, get is O(1).
  • Redis does the same idea: lazy expiry on access plus a periodic job sampling keys with TTLs.
fields.Hint: Lazy check on read plus a min heap of expiry times.
fields.Fact: Combine lazy expiry for correctness with background sweeping for memory.
fields.Source:
Redis: Key eviction (https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/reference/eviction/)
Python documentation: heapq (https://docs.python.org/3/library/heapq.html)

fields.Question: Design the home news feed for a social network with 300M DAU. Users follow others; the feed shows recent posts from people they follow.
fields.Answer:
• APIs: POST /posts, GET /feed?cursor=&limit=20.
  • Services: post service (writes posts to a sharded store keyed by post_id, with an author index), graph service (follows), fanout service, feed service, media in object storage plus CDN.
  • Feed storage: per user list of post ids in Redis (or a wide column table) capped at ~800 entries: feed:{user_id} -> [post_id ...]. Hydrate post bodies and authors from caches at read time.
  • Write path: post saved, event to a queue, fanout workers push the post id into each follower's feed list.

Key decision: fanout on write versus read

  • Push (fanout on write): fast reads, but a celebrity with 50M followers creates 50M writes per post and wasted work for inactive users.
  • Pull (fanout on read): no write amplification, but every feed read merges many timelines; slow.
  • Hybrid: push for normal accounts, pull for accounts above a follower threshold, merge at read time. Skip fanout to users inactive for weeks; rebuild their feed on next login.

Other deep dives: ranking (fetch candidates, score with a model, cache result), cursor pagination by post id or score, deletes (filter at hydration time), consistency (author sees own post immediately by merging it in client side or server side).
fields.Hint: Hybrid push for most users, pull for celebrities.
fields.Fact: Feed design is a fanout tradeoff: write amplification versus read latency, split by follower count.
fields.Source:
System Design Interview: An Insider's Guide, Volume 1 (https://bytebytego.com/)
The Infrastructure Behind Twitter: Scale (https://blog.x.com/engineering/en_us/topics/infrastructure/2017/the-infrastructure-behind-twitter-scale)
TAO: Facebook's Distributed Data Store for the Social Graph (https://www.usenix.org/conference/atc13/technical-sessions/presentation/bronson)

fields.Question: Coding: for a fanout on read feed, merge the k followed users' timelines (each already sorted newest first) and return the newest n posts.
fields.Answer:
import heapq

def merge_feeds(timelines, n):
    heap = []
    for i, tl in enumerate(timelines):
        if tl:
            post = tl[0]
            heapq.heappush(heap, (-post.created_at, i, 0))
    result = []
    while heap and len(result) < n:
        _, i, j = heapq.heappop(heap)
        result.append(timelines[i][j])
        if j + 1 < len(timelines[i]):
            nxt = timelines[i][j + 1]
            heapq.heappush(heap, (-nxt.created_at, i, j + 1))
    return result
  • Time O(k + n log k), space O(k). Negate timestamps because heapq is a min heap; the index i breaks ties so posts are never compared.
  • In production each timeline is fetched lazily in pages, and you only fetch the first page per followee.
  • For pagination, return a cursor (last created_at and post_id) and resume from it rather than using offsets.
  • heapq.merge(*timelines, key=..., reverse=True) does this lazily in one line.
fields.Hint: Min heap of the head of each list.
fields.Fact: K way merge with a heap is the core of fanout on read.
fields.Source:
Python documentation: heapq (https://docs.python.org/3/library/heapq.html)
System Design Interview: An Insider's Guide, Volume 1 (https://bytebytego.com/)

fields.Question: In your push based feed, a user with 80M followers posts. Fanout workers fall hours behind and everyone's feed is stale. What do you change?
fields.Answer:
• Do not fan out for accounts above a threshold (say 100k followers). Store their posts only in their own timeline.
  • At feed read time, fetch the reader's precomputed feed plus the recent posts of the few celebrities they follow, merge, rank, cache briefly.
  • Cache celebrity timelines aggressively; they are read by millions, so it is a hot key: replicate it or use local caches.
  • Prioritize fanout queues: active users first, skip users inactive for N days.
  • Separate fanout worker pools so a celebrity burst cannot starve normal fanout.

Tradeoff: read path gets slightly more expensive for users who follow celebrities, in exchange for bounded write amplification. Monitor fanout lag as an SLO.
fields.Hint: Treat celebrities as pull.
fields.Fact: Bound write amplification by switching high follower accounts to fanout on read.
fields.Source:
System Design Interview: An Insider's Guide, Volume 1 (https://bytebytego.com/)
The Infrastructure Behind Twitter: Scale (https://blog.x.com/engineering/en_us/topics/infrastructure/2017/the-infrastructure-behind-twitter-scale)

fields.Question: Design a chat app like WhatsApp or Messenger: 1:1 and group chats, online presence, message history, delivery receipts, 500M DAU.
fields.Answer:
• Connection: clients hold a persistent WebSocket to a chat gateway. Gateways are stateful; a session service maps user_id -> gateway (in Redis) so others can route to them.
  • Send path: client sends message with a client generated id; gateway forwards to the chat service, which assigns a per conversation sequence or Snowflake id, persists it, acks the sender, then routes to recipients' gateways. If a recipient is offline, enqueue a push notification.
  • Storage: wide column store partitioned by conversation_id (bucketed by time for huge groups), clustered by message id. Append heavy, read by recent range. Discord moved from Cassandra to ScyllaDB with this model.
  • Sync: each device tracks the last message id per conversation it has; on reconnect it fetches everything after it. This handles multiple devices.
  • Receipts: sent (server persisted), delivered (device acked), read (user opened), sent as small events on the same channel.
  • Presence: heartbeats to a presence service with a TTL; publish changes only to friends who are online, and debounce flapping.

Scale and failures: millions of connections per region means many gateways (each can hold ~100k to 1M idle connections). On gateway crash clients reconnect with backoff and resync. Groups: fan out to members' gateways; for very large groups, fan out through a queue. End to end encryption means the server stores ciphertext only.
fields.Hint: WebSocket gateways, session registry, per conversation ordered store.
fields.Fact: Chat is routing over persistent connections plus an ordered, resumable message log per conversation.
fields.Source:
System Design Interview: An Insider's Guide, Volume 1 (https://bytebytego.com/)
How Discord Stores Trillions of Messages (https://discord.com/blog/how-discord-stores-trillions-of-messages)
RFC 6455: The WebSocket Protocol (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6455)

fields.Question: In your chat design, how do you guarantee messages in a conversation are shown in the same order on every device, with no duplicates or gaps, despite retries and reconnects?
fields.Answer:
• Server assigned order: the conversation's owner (one partition or one leader per conversation) assigns a monotonically increasing sequence number at persist time. Client clocks are never trusted for order.
  • Dedup: client attaches a client message id (UUID); the server stores it with a unique constraint per conversation, so a retried send returns the existing sequence number.
  • Gap detection: devices track the last sequence received. If they get seq 105 after 102, they fetch 103 and 104 from history. On reconnect they ask for everything after their last seq.
  • At least once delivery from server to device, deduped on the device by sequence number.
  • Optimistic UI: show the sent message locally as pending, then reorder it once the server seq arrives.

Tradeoff: a single sequencer per conversation limits throughput per conversation, which is fine (humans type slowly); conversations are spread across partitions. Global order across conversations is unnecessary.
fields.Hint: Per conversation sequence numbers plus client message ids.
fields.Fact: Order per conversation from one sequencer; dedupe with client ids; repair gaps from history.
fields.Source:
System Design Interview: An Insider's Guide, Volume 1 (https://bytebytego.com/)
Apache Kafka Documentation (https://kafka.apache.org/documentation/)
Designing Data-Intensive Applications (https://dataintensive.net/)

fields.Question: Why WebSockets for chat instead of HTTP polling or long polling? What are the operational problems with WebSockets at scale?
fields.Answer:
• Polling: simple but wasteful and adds latency equal to the poll interval.
  • Long polling: server holds the request until a message arrives; better latency, but reconnect per message and awkward for sending.
  • Server sent events: server to client stream over HTTP; good for notifications, client still uses HTTP to send.
  • WebSocket: full duplex over one TCP connection after an HTTP upgrade; low overhead per message, true push.

Operational problems

  • Stateful connections: load balancers must support long lived connections; deploys must drain gateways gracefully and clients must reconnect with jittered backoff to avoid a reconnect storm.
  • Routing: you need a registry of which gateway holds which user.
  • Idle mobile connections die silently: application level heartbeats and fast resync on reconnect.
  • Mobile background: the OS kills sockets, so offline delivery relies on APNs or FCM push.
fields.Hint: Full duplex push over one connection.
fields.Fact: WebSockets give low latency push but make the gateway tier stateful.
fields.Source:
RFC 6455: The WebSocket Protocol (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6455)
System Design Interview: An Insider's Guide, Volume 1 (https://bytebytego.com/)

fields.Question: Design a notification system that sends push (iOS and Android), SMS and email for many internal services, around 10M notifications per day with spikes.
fields.Answer:
• API: internal services call POST /notify {user_id, template_id, params, channels?, idempotency_key, priority}.
  • Notification service: validates, checks user preferences and opt outs, rate limits per user, renders the template, then enqueues one message per channel.
  • Queues per channel (push iOS, push Android, SMS, email) so a slow SMS vendor cannot block push. Separate high priority (OTP, security) from bulk (marketing).
  • Channel workers call providers: APNs, FCM, an SMS provider, an email provider. Retries with backoff for transient errors; dead letter queue for permanent ones.
  • Data: device tokens per user (remove tokens the provider reports invalid), preferences, a notification log with status for audit and dedup.

Deep dives: dedup by idempotency key (at least once queues will redeliver), ordering is rarely needed, delivery tracking via provider callbacks and open tracking, scheduling and time zone aware quiet hours, a kill switch for bad campaigns, and analytics events to a stream.

Pitfall: providers do not guarantee delivery; APNs and FCM are best effort, so critical flows (OTP) need a fallback channel.
fields.Hint: Preferences and rate limits, then a queue per channel.
fields.Fact: Isolate channels and priorities with separate queues and make every worker idempotent.

fields.Question: Users complain they got the same push notification three times. Your pipeline uses queues with at least once delivery. Where do duplicates come from and how do you stop them?
fields.Answer:
• Sources: the upstream service retried the API call; the queue redelivered after a worker crashed before acking or exceeded its visibility timeout; the worker retried a provider call that actually succeeded but timed out.
  • Fix at the API: require an idempotency key per logical notification; store it with a unique constraint and return the existing result on repeat.
  • Fix at the worker: before sending, atomically mark (notification_id, channel) as sending (SET NX with TTL or a conditional insert); skip if already sent. Record sent after the provider accepts.
  • Visibility timeout longer than the p99 processing time; extend it for long jobs.
  • Use provider level collapse or dedup ids where they exist (APNs apns-collapse-id, FCM collapse keys) so retries replace instead of stacking.

Tradeoff: there is still a tiny window (provider accepted, worker crashed before recording) that can duplicate. Accept it for push; for money or OTP use stronger end to end idempotency.
fields.Hint: Idempotency keys at the API and dedup at the worker.
fields.Fact: At least once pipelines need explicit dedup at every hop that causes side effects.

fields.Question: Design a web crawler that fetches 1 billion pages per month for a search index.
fields.Answer:
Estimates: 1B/month is ~400 pages/s average, plan ~1,000/s peak. At ~500 KB per page that is ~500 TB/month raw, so compress and store in object storage.

  • Components: seed URLs, URL frontier, fetcher workers, DNS resolver with cache, content parser, content dedup, URL extractor, URL filter and dedup, storage.
  • Loop: frontier gives a URL; fetcher checks robots.txt (cached per host), downloads; parser extracts text and links; content hash checked against seen content; new links normalized, filtered, checked against seen URLs, then added to the frontier.
  • URL frontier: front queues by priority (PageRank, freshness), back queues one per host, so each host is fetched by one worker with a delay between requests (politeness).
  • Dedup: seen URL set of billions of entries: Bloom filter in memory or a sharded KV of URL hashes. Content dedup with a hash (exact) or SimHash (near duplicates).
  • Distribution: partition the frontier by host hash so one host maps to one worker group.

Robustness: spider traps (infinite calendars, session ids in URLs): cap depth and URL length, limit pages per host. Timeouts per fetch, retry with backoff, checkpoint the frontier so a crash resumes. Recrawl scheduling by observed change rate.
fields.Hint: Frontier with per host queues, dedup URLs and content.
fields.Fact: A crawler is a distributed BFS whose hard parts are politeness, dedup and traps.
fields.Source:
System Design Interview: An Insider's Guide, Volume 1 (https://bytebytego.com/)
Mercator: A Scalable, Extensible Web Crawler (https://doi.org/10.1023/A:1019213109274)

fields.Question: Coding: write a single process crawler that does BFS from a start URL, stays on the same host, never fetches a URL twice, and stops after max_pages. Assume fetch(url) returns HTML and extract_links(html, base) returns absolute URLs.
fields.Answer:
from collections import deque
from urllib.parse import urldefrag, urlparse

def normalize(url):
    url, _ = urldefrag(url)
    return url.rstrip("/")

def crawl(start, max_pages=1000):
    host = urlparse(start).netloc
    start = normalize(start)
    seen = {start}
    queue = deque([start])
    pages = {}
    while queue and len(pages) < max_pages:
        url = queue.popleft()
        try:
            html = fetch(url)
        except Exception:
            continue
        pages[url] = html
        for link in extract_links(html, url):
            link = normalize(link)
            if urlparse(link).netloc == host and link not in seen:
                seen.add(link)
                queue.append(link)
    return pages
  • Mark URLs seen when enqueued, not when fetched, so a URL is never queued twice.
  • O(V + E) over pages and links; memory O(V) for the seen set.
  • Follow up, concurrency: a thread pool or asyncio with a semaphore; protect seen with a lock or do dedup in the single coordinator.
  • Follow up, politeness: honor robots.txt and a per host delay; with one host, a global rate limiter.
fields.Hint: BFS with a seen set; mark on enqueue.
fields.Fact: Dedup on enqueue and normalize URLs, or the crawl explodes.
fields.Source:
Mercator: A Scalable, Extensible Web Crawler (https://doi.org/10.1023/A:1019213109274)
RFC 9309: Robots Exclusion Protocol (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9309)

fields.Question: Your crawler with 1,000 workers gets your IP range blocked by several sites within an hour. What do you change?
fields.Answer:
• Honor robots.txt (RFC 9309): fetch and cache it per host, obey disallow rules and any crawl delay.
  • One back queue per host, assigned to a single worker, with a minimum delay between requests to that host (often a multiple of the last fetch time).
  • Limit concurrent connections per host and per IP (many hosts share an IP on shared hosting).
  • Identify yourself with a clear User-Agent and contact URL.
  • Back off on 429 and 503, respect Retry-After, and lower the rate for hosts that respond slowly.
  • Spread load across the day, recrawl only pages that change.

Design point: politeness is why the frontier maps hosts to queues; you cannot just shard URLs randomly across workers.
fields.Hint: One queue per host, delay between fetches.
fields.Fact: Crawl throughput comes from many hosts in parallel, never from hammering one host.

fields.Question: Design search autocomplete: as the user types, return the top 5 most popular completions for the prefix within 100 ms, for 10M DAU.
fields.Answer:
• Estimates: 10M users x 10 searches x ~5 keystrokes is ~500M requests/day, ~6k QPS average, ~12k peak. Read heavy, latency critical.
  • Data structure: a trie where each node caches the top k completions for its prefix. Query is O(length of prefix) plus O(k), no subtree traversal.
  • Build pipeline: search logs go to a stream, aggregated (for example weekly, or with decay for trending) into (query, count). An offline job builds the trie and publishes a snapshot. Serving nodes load it in memory.
  • Serving: shard by prefix (first one or two characters, rebalanced by traffic since letters are uneven) or replicate the full trie if it fits in memory. Cache popular prefixes at the CDN and in the browser; debounce keystrokes on the client.
  • Freshness: rebuild periodically; for trending queries, a separate real time layer with a smaller trie merged at query time.

Also mention: filtering offensive or blocked terms in the build step and at serving, personalization (merge with the user's history), multiple languages, and typo tolerance (fuzzy matching) as a follow up.
fields.Hint: Trie with top k cached per node, built offline.
fields.Fact: Precompute top k per prefix so serving is a constant time lookup.
fields.Source:

fields.Question: Coding: build a structure from (query, count) pairs that returns the top k queries for any prefix. Optimize for fast queries.
fields.Answer:
import heapq

class Node:
    __slots__ = ("children", "top")
    def __init__(self):
        self.children = {}
        self.top = []

class Autocomplete:
    def __init__(self, counts: dict, k: int = 5):
        self.root = Node()
        self.k = k
        for query, count in counts.items():
            node = self.root
            for ch in query:
                node = node.children.setdefault(ch, Node())
                node.top.append((count, query))
        self._trim(self.root)

    def _trim(self, node):
        node.top = [q for _, q in heapq.nlargest(self.k, node.top)]
        for child in node.children.values():
            self._trim(child)

    def suggest(self, prefix: str):
        node = self.root
        for ch in prefix:
            node = node.children.get(ch)
            if node is None:
                return []
        return node.top
  • Query O(p) for prefix length p, results already sorted.
  • Build O(total characters x log k) with nlargest; memory O(total characters x k) because each node stores up to k strings (store ids instead of strings to save space).
  • Trade off: storing top k per node costs memory but avoids traversing a subtree on every keystroke.
  • Follow up: updates. Rebuilding offline and swapping snapshots is simpler than updating top k lists along the path for each count change.
  • Deep recursion on long queries: use an explicit stack in _trim if queries can exceed Python's recursion limit.
fields.Hint: Cache top k at every trie node.
fields.Fact: Precomputing results at each node moves cost from query time to build time.
fields.Source:
System Design Interview: An Insider's Guide, Volume 1 (https://bytebytego.com/)
Python documentation: heapq (https://docs.python.org/3/library/heapq.html)

fields.Question: Design a service that returns the top 100 most viewed videos in the last hour, the last day, and all time, with billions of view events per day.
fields.Answer:
• Ingest: view events to Kafka, partitioned by video_id so counts for one video land on one partition.
  • Aggregate: stream processors (Flink, Kafka Streams) keep per video counts in tumbling windows (for example 1 minute), emit (window, video_id, count).
  • Per partition top k: each processor keeps a min heap of size k over its videos; a final stage merges the per partition top k lists into the global top k. This is correct because each video lives on exactly one partition.
  • Sliding windows: last hour = sum of the last 60 minute buckets; store bucket counts and recompute top k every minute.
  • Serving: write results to a cache keyed by window; reads are trivial.

Approximation follow up: if memory per processor is too high, use Count-Min Sketch plus a heap of candidates (overestimates only, error bounded), or the Space-Saving algorithm. Mention the lambda style split: fast approximate stream results corrected by an exact batch job.
fields.Hint: Partition by key, heap per partition, merge.
fields.Fact: Exact distributed top k works when each key is counted on exactly one partition.
fields.Source:

fields.Question: Coding: given a stream of item ids, return the k most frequent. Then do it when the list is huge and k is small.
fields.Answer:
import heapq
from collections import Counter

def top_k(items, k):
    counts = Counter(items)
    return heapq.nlargest(k, counts, key=counts.__getitem__)
  • Counting O(n), selection O(m log k) for m distinct items, memory O(m + k).
  • Alternative O(n) selection: bucket sort by frequency (index = count), walk buckets from the top.
  • If distinct items do not fit in memory: hash partition items into files or machines by id, compute top k per partition, merge the partial lists (exact, because each id is in one partition).
  • If even that is too costly: Count-Min Sketch for approximate counts with a heap of size k for candidates.
fields.Hint: Counter plus a size k heap.
fields.Fact: Count, then select with a k sized heap; partition by key to scale out.
fields.Source: Python documentation: heapq (https://docs.python.org/3/library/heapq.html)

fields.Question: Design a file storage and sync service like Dropbox or Google Drive: upload, download, sync across devices, share, version history. 50M DAU.
fields.Answer:
• Split metadata from blobs. Blobs (file chunks) go to object storage (S3 or similar); metadata (files, folders, versions, chunk lists, permissions) goes to a relational DB sharded by user or namespace.
  • Chunking: client splits files into blocks (for example 4 MB), hashes each (SHA-256). A file version is an ordered list of chunk hashes.
  • Upload: client sends the chunk hash list; the server replies which chunks it does not have; client uploads only those (directly to object storage via presigned URLs); then commits the new version to metadata.
  • Sync: each namespace has a monotonically increasing change journal. Devices hold a cursor and long poll or subscribe to a notification service; on change they fetch entries after their cursor and download missing chunks.
  • Conflicts: two devices edit the same base version. Commit with optimistic concurrency (expected parent version); the loser gets a conflicted copy rather than silent overwrite.
  • Sharing: ACL rows per file or folder; links with tokens.

Benefits of chunks: resumable uploads, delta sync (only changed chunks), dedup across versions and users. Durability: object storage replicates across AZs; metadata DB has backups and replicas. Cold versions move to cheaper storage tiers.
fields.Hint: Metadata DB plus content addressed chunks in object storage.
fields.Fact: Content addressed chunks give dedup, delta sync and resumable uploads for free.
fields.Source:

fields.Question: Users upload 20 GB files over flaky mobile and home connections. How do you make uploads reliable and not route the bytes through your app servers?
fields.Answer:
• Presigned URLs: the API authorizes the upload and returns short lived signed URLs; the client uploads directly to object storage. App servers never touch the bytes.
  • Multipart upload: initiate an upload id, upload parts (S3 allows 5 MB to 5 GB per part, up to 10,000 parts) in parallel, then complete with the part list. Failed parts are retried individually.
  • Resume: client persists the upload id and finished parts; on restart it lists uploaded parts and continues.
  • Integrity: per part checksums, plus a whole file hash checked at completion.
  • Commit: storage emits an event (or client calls complete); metadata is written only after the object exists, so no dangling metadata.
  • Cleanup: lifecycle rule to abort incomplete multipart uploads after N days, otherwise you pay for orphaned parts.

Follow ups: virus scanning and processing asynchronously after upload, quotas checked before issuing URLs, rate limiting part uploads.
fields.Hint: Presigned multipart uploads straight to object storage.
fields.Fact: Keep large bytes off your servers and make each part independently retryable.
fields.Source:
Amazon S3: Uploading and copying objects using multipart upload (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/mpuoverview.html)

fields.Question: Design a video platform like YouTube: creators upload videos, viewers stream them on any device with minimal buffering. 1B views per day.
fields.Answer:
• Upload path: client uploads the original to object storage (presigned multipart). An event starts a transcoding pipeline.
  • Transcoding: split the video into segments, transcode in parallel on a worker fleet into a bitrate ladder (240p to 4K) and codecs (H.264, VP9, AV1), produce thumbnails, run content checks. Model it as a DAG of tasks driven by a queue; retries per task.
  • Packaging: HLS or DASH: small segments (2 to 6 s) plus manifests listing the renditions.
  • Serving: segments are immutable, so cache them on a CDN with long TTLs. Popular videos are served almost entirely from edge; the long tail from origin or regional caches. Netflix places its own cache appliances inside ISPs (Open Connect).
  • Metadata: video info, channel, counts in a sharded DB plus caches; view counts aggregated asynchronously.
  • Playback: the player picks renditions with adaptive bitrate based on measured throughput and buffer level.

Estimates: egress dominates cost. 1B views x ~5 min x ~3 Mbps average is about 1B x 112 MB, ~100 PB/day, which is why the CDN and codec efficiency are the key decisions.
fields.Hint: Transcode to a bitrate ladder, segment, serve from CDN.
fields.Fact: Video at scale is a CDN and transcoding problem; the app servers barely see the bytes.
fields.Source:
System Design Interview: An Insider's Guide, Volume 1 (https://bytebytego.com/)

Netflix Open Connect (https://openconnect.netflix.com/en/)

fields.Question: Viewers on mobile complain of constant buffering, while desktop users are fine. How does adaptive bitrate streaming fix this, and what would you tune?
fields.Answer:
• The video is encoded at several bitrates and cut into short segments; a manifest (HLS m3u8 or DASH MPD) lists them.
  • The player downloads segment by segment and, before each, chooses a rendition based on recent throughput and how many seconds are buffered. Low bandwidth drops to 360p instead of stalling.
  • Because segments align across renditions, switching happens at segment boundaries without glitches.

Tuning

  • Start at a conservative bitrate for fast startup, then ramp up.
  • Buffer based switching (like BOLA) is more stable than throughput only on fluctuating mobile networks.
  • Shorter segments adapt faster but cost more requests and less compression efficiency.
  • Add lower rungs to the ladder for weak networks, and per title encoding so simple content uses lower bitrates.
  • Measure rebuffer ratio, startup time and average bitrate as the user facing metrics.
fields.Hint: Multiple renditions, player switches per segment.
fields.Fact: ABR trades picture quality for continuous playback by switching renditions per segment.
fields.Source:
RFC 8216: HTTP Live Streaming (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8216)

fields.Question: Design a ride sharing service like Uber: riders request a ride, nearby drivers are matched, both see live location. 1M active drivers sending location every 4 seconds.
fields.Answer:
Estimates: 1M / 4 s = 250k location updates per second. That write rate decides the design: do not write every update to a durable relational DB.

  • Location service: drivers send updates over a persistent connection. Store the latest location in memory, indexed geospatially (geohash or H3 cell -> set of driver ids), in Redis or a sharded in memory service partitioned by cell. TTL so stale drivers drop out. Stream raw updates to Kafka for trip history and analytics.
  • Matching: on a ride request, look up drivers in the rider's cell and neighboring cells, filter by availability, rank by ETA (road network, not straight line), offer to the best driver with a short timeout, then the next.
  • Consistency for assignment: a driver must not get two rides. Use a conditional update on driver state (available -> offered) or a per driver lock with a lease.
  • Trip service: trip state machine (requested, matched, en route, in progress, completed, paid) in a transactional DB.
  • Live tracking: push driver location to the rider over WebSocket via the gateway.
  • Pricing: surge computed per cell from supply and demand over short windows.

Deep dives: hot cells in dense downtowns (smaller cells or split shards), region isolation (each city is mostly independent, shard by city), failover of the in memory index (rebuild from the next round of updates within seconds).
fields.Hint: In memory geospatial index of latest locations, sharded by cell.
fields.Fact: High frequency location writes belong in memory with a TTL; durable storage is only for trips.
fields.Source:
