fields.Question: How do you find all drivers within 2 km of a rider efficiently? Compare geohash, quadtree and H3.
fields.Answer:
• Geohash: encodes lat and lng into a string where a shared prefix means nearby. Precision 6 cells are about 1.2 km x 0.6 km. Query the rider's cell plus its 8 neighbors (needed because nearby points can fall across a cell edge), then filter by exact distance. Easy to store as a key in Redis or a DB index. Redis GEO commands use geohash internally.
  • Quadtree: recursively split regions until each leaf holds at most N points; adapts to density (small cells downtown, large in rural areas). Good for static points of interest; costly to keep updated with fast moving drivers.
  • H3: Uber's hierarchical hexagonal grid. Hexagons have uniform neighbor distances (all 6 neighbors equidistant), which makes k ring searches and aggregation like surge pricing cleaner.

Answer for drivers: fixed cells (geohash or H3) in memory, because updates are cheap: on each location update move the driver between cell sets only if the cell changed. Then do a radius search over a ring of cells, sort by distance or ETA.

Pitfalls: forgetting neighbor cells, geohash distortion near poles, and using straight line distance as the final ranking for pickup ETA.
fields.Hint: Cells plus neighbors, then exact filter.
fields.Fact: Grid cells turn a 2D proximity search into a few key lookups.

fields.Question: Design the payment system for an e-commerce site: customers pay at checkout through an external payment processor (Stripe, Adyen), and merchants are paid out later.
fields.Answer:
• Flow: checkout creates a payment order with an idempotency key, status created. The payment service calls the processor (usually through a hosted payment page or tokenized card so you never store raw card numbers, reducing PCI scope). The processor returns success, failure or pending; final results also arrive by webhook.
  • State machine: created, pending, succeeded, failed, refunded. Transitions are idempotent and persisted before side effects.
  • Ledger: every money movement is recorded as double entry ledger rows (debit one account, credit another, sums to zero), append only. Balances are derived.
  • Wallet or balances for merchants updated from the ledger; payouts run as scheduled batch jobs.
  • Reliability: idempotency keys on our API and passed to the processor; retries with backoff; webhooks deduped by event id; outbox for publishing payment events.
  • Reconciliation: nightly compare our ledger against the processor's settlement files; mismatches go to a queue for investigation.

Consistency: strong consistency in a relational DB with transactions. Availability is secondary to correctness: better to fail a payment than to double charge. Timeouts are unknown state, not failure: query the processor before retrying.
fields.Hint: Idempotent state machine, double entry ledger, reconciliation.
fields.Fact: Payments prioritize correctness: idempotency everywhere, append only ledger, and reconciliation as the safety net.
fields.Source:

fields.Question: Coding and design: implement transfer(from_account, to_account, amount) for a wallet service so balances never go negative, no money is created or lost, and retries are safe.
fields.Answer:
def transfer(db, transfer_id, src, dst, amount_cents):
    if amount_cents <= 0 or src == dst:
        raise ValueError("invalid transfer")
    with db.transaction():
        if db.exists("transfers", id=transfer_id):
            return "duplicate"
        first, second = sorted([src, dst])
        accounts = {a: db.select_for_update("accounts", id=a) for a in (first, second)}
        if accounts[src].balance < amount_cents:
            raise InsufficientFunds()
        db.insert("transfers", id=transfer_id, src=src, dst=dst, amount=amount_cents)
        db.insert("entries", transfer_id=transfer_id, account=src, amount=-amount_cents)
        db.insert("entries", transfer_id=transfer_id, account=dst, amount=amount_cents)
        db.update("accounts", src, balance=accounts[src].balance - amount_cents)
        db.update("accounts", dst, balance=accounts[dst].balance + amount_cents)
    return "ok"
  • Integer cents (or a decimal type), never floats.
  • Lock both rows in a consistent order (sorted ids) to avoid deadlocks between opposite transfers.
  • transfer_id with a primary key makes retries idempotent; a concurrent duplicate fails on the unique constraint and is treated as duplicate.
  • Double entry rows sum to zero per transfer, so audits can verify no money was created.
  • Add a DB check constraint balance >= 0 as a last line of defense.

Across shards: if accounts live on different databases you cannot use one transaction: use a saga (debit with a hold, credit, then finalize, with compensation) driven by a durable workflow.
fields.Hint: One transaction, ordered row locks, unique transfer id.
fields.Fact: Money moves as balanced, idempotent, atomic ledger entries in integer units.
fields.Source:

Designing Data-Intensive Applications (https://dataintensive.net/)

fields.Question: Your service calls the payment processor to charge a card and the request times out after 30 seconds. What do you do?
fields.Answer:
A timeout is an unknown outcome, not a failure. The charge may have succeeded.

  • Mark the payment pending_unknown; never tell the user it failed yet.
  • Retry with the same idempotency key: the processor returns the original result instead of charging again.
  • Or query the processor's status API for that payment, and also wait for the webhook.
  • A background job resolves stuck pending payments after a timeout, using the status API.
  • Show the user a processing state and notify them when it resolves.
  • Reconciliation against settlement reports catches anything still inconsistent.

Pitfall: retrying with a new idempotency key, or marking failed and letting the user click pay again, both risk double charging.
fields.Hint: Unknown, not failed: retry with the same key.
fields.Fact: Treat timeouts on side effecting calls as unknown and resolve them idempotently.
fields.Source:

Designing robust and predictable APIs with idempotency (https://stripe.com/blog/idempotency)

fields.Question: Design flash sale or ticket booking: 10,000 seats, 1M users hitting buy at the same second. No seat may be sold twice.
fields.Answer:
• Absorb the spike: CDN for static pages, a virtual waiting room or queue that admits users at a controlled rate, rate limit per user, bot protection.
  • Reserve then pay: selecting a seat creates a hold with a short expiry (for example 10 min). Holding is a conditional update: UPDATE seats SET status = 'held', holder = ?, hold_until = now() + interval '10 min' WHERE id = ? AND (status = 'free' OR (status = 'held' AND hold_until < now())); affected rows = 1 means you got it.
  • Unnumbered inventory: a single counter is a hot row; pre split it into N buckets or decrement atomically in Redis (DECR, or a Lua script that refuses below zero) and persist reservations asynchronously with reconciliation.
  • Payment: confirm with an idempotency key; on success mark sold; on expiry release the hold.
  • Fairness: the waiting room gives first come ordering instead of whoever retries fastest.

Pitfalls: read then write without a condition (oversell), long DB transactions held across the payment call, and letting retries from impatient users multiply load.
fields.Hint: Conditional update to hold, then pay, with expiry.
fields.Fact: Prevent overselling with atomic conditional writes; control the stampede with an admission queue.
fields.Source:
System Design Interview: An Insider's Guide, Volume 2 (https://bytebytego.com/)
Designing Data-Intensive Applications (https://dataintensive.net/)
PostgreSQL: Transaction Isolation (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/transaction-iso.html)

fields.Question: Design a real time leaderboard for a game with 50M players: update scores, show the top 100, and show any player's rank.
fields.Answer:
• Redis sorted set: ZADD lb score player (or ZINCRBY), top 100 with ZREVRANGE lb 0 99 WITHSCORES, rank with ZREVRANK lb player. All O(log n), backed by a skip list.
  • 50M members at ~100 bytes each is ~5 GB: fits on one node; replicate for reads and persist (AOF or snapshots) or rebuild from the score DB.
  • Durable source of truth: score events in a DB or log; Redis is the index.
  • Ties: encode a tiebreak in the score so earlier achievers rank higher, for example score x 2^32 + (2^32 - 1 - seconds_since_season_start). Redis scores are doubles, so keep the combined value under 2^53 to stay exact.
  • Periods: one sorted set per day or season (lb:2026-10), expire old ones.

Beyond one node: shard by score range (rank = count in higher shards + local rank) or shard by player and merge per shard top 100 for the top list; exact global rank across player shards needs counting, so approximate rank with score histograms for the long tail. Pitfall: computing rank with ORDER BY score and OFFSET in SQL on every request.
fields.Hint: Sorted set: ZADD, ZREVRANGE, ZREVRANK.
fields.Fact: A skip list backed sorted set gives log n updates, top k and rank queries.
fields.Source:
System Design Interview: An Insider's Guide, Volume 2 (https://bytebytego.com/)
Redis: Key eviction (https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/reference/eviction/)

fields.Question: Design a distributed job scheduler (like cron at scale): users schedule millions of jobs to run at specific times or intervals; each run should happen once.
fields.Answer:
• Storage: jobs table (definition, schedule) and a runs table indexed by next_run_at, partitioned so many schedulers can poll different partitions.
  • Dispatch: scheduler workers poll due runs (SELECT ... WHERE next_run_at <= now() ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED LIMIT 100), mark them dispatched, enqueue them, and compute the next run time in the same transaction.
  • Execution: executors consume the queue, run the job, record status. Heartbeats with leases: if an executor dies, the lease expires and the run is retried.
  • Once semantics: delivery is at least once, so the job itself takes a run id and must be idempotent; the runs table has a unique (job_id, scheduled_time).
  • Precision: for second level precision, load runs due in the next minute into an in memory timing wheel or delay queue.

Follow ups: missed runs after downtime (catch up or skip policy), time zones and DST for cron expressions, rate limiting per tenant, retries with backoff and a max attempt count, observability of late runs.
fields.Hint: Poll due runs with SKIP LOCKED, lease based execution.
fields.Fact: Scheduling is a durable priority queue by time plus idempotent, lease based execution.
fields.Source:
Designing Data-Intensive Applications (https://dataintensive.net/)
Amazon SQS Developer Guide (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/welcome.html)

fields.Question: Design a metrics and monitoring system (like Prometheus or Datadog) ingesting 10M data points per second from 100k hosts, with dashboards and alerts.
fields.Answer:
• Data model: series identified by metric name plus labels; points are (timestamp, value).
  • Ingest: agents batch and push (or a pull model where the server scrapes); a stateless ingest tier writes to Kafka for buffering, then to a time series DB.
  • Storage: time series DB sharded by series id hash, data in time partitioned blocks with delta of delta timestamps and XOR float compression (Gorilla style, ~1.4 bytes per point). Recent data in memory, older on disk or object storage.
  • Downsampling: keep raw for days, 1 minute rollups for weeks, 1 hour for a year.
  • Query: fan out to shards holding the series, aggregate; cache dashboard queries.
  • Alerting: rule evaluator queries periodically; alert manager dedupes, groups, routes and silences.

Pitfalls: label cardinality explosions (user_id as a label creates millions of series and kills memory); alerting pipeline depending on the same infrastructure it monitors (run it separately, add a dead man's switch).
fields.Hint: Push to a buffer, sharded compressed time series storage, rollups.
fields.Fact: Series cardinality, not point volume, is what usually breaks a metrics system.
fields.Source:
Site Reliability Engineering: Service Level Objectives (https://sre.google/sre-book/service-level-objectives/)
Apache Kafka Documentation (https://kafka.apache.org/documentation/)
Designing Data-Intensive Applications (https://dataintensive.net/)

fields.Question: Design keyword search over 1 billion documents (posts or products) returning the top 20 relevant results in under 200 ms.
fields.Answer:
• Inverted index: term -> posting list of (doc_id, term frequency, positions). Built by tokenizing, normalizing (lowercase, stemming) each document.
  • Sharding by document: each shard indexes a subset of docs; a query fans out to all shards, each returns its local top k by score (BM25 plus signals), and a coordinator merges. Replicas per shard for throughput.
  • Indexing pipeline: source DB changes via CDC or events to a queue, indexers update near real time (Elasticsearch style refresh every second); segments are immutable and merged in the background.
  • Ranking: cheap first pass (BM25) over candidates, expensive second pass (ML model) on the top few hundred.

Tradeoffs: document sharding means every query hits every shard (tail latency is the max of shards, so hedge or set timeouts and return partial results). Term sharding hits fewer shards but makes multi term queries and hot terms hard. The search index is eventually consistent with the source of truth.
fields.Hint: Inverted index sharded by document, scatter gather top k.
fields.Fact: Search is scatter gather over document sharded inverted indexes with two stage ranking.
fields.Source:
Designing Data-Intensive Applications (https://dataintensive.net/)
Elasticsearch: Completion suggester (https://www.elastic.co/guide/en/elasticsearch/reference/current/search-suggesters.html)

fields.Question: In a Pastebin or URL shortener, pastes expire after a user chosen time. How do you delete billions of expired items efficiently?
fields.Answer:
• Lazy: check expires_at on read and return 404 if expired. Correctness never depends on cleanup.
  • Background cleanup: a batch job scans an index on expires_at and deletes in small batches to avoid long locks and replication lag spikes.
  • Store native TTL: Cassandra, DynamoDB and Redis can expire rows themselves (DynamoDB deletes asynchronously, so still check on read).
  • Partition by time: if most items share fixed TTLs, put them in daily partitions or tables and drop whole partitions, which is far cheaper than row deletes.
  • Blobs: object storage lifecycle rules delete content by prefix or tag.

Pitfall: one giant DELETE WHERE expires_at < now() that locks tables and floods replicas.
fields.Hint: Lazy check on read plus batched or partition based cleanup.
fields.Fact: Make expiry correct at read time and cheap in the background.
fields.Source:
System Design Interview: An Insider's Guide, Volume 1 (https://bytebytego.com/)
Designing Data-Intensive Applications (https://dataintensive.net/)

fields.Question: Coding: implement a Bloom filter for the crawler's "have we seen this URL" check, and explain how to size it.
fields.Answer:
import hashlib, math

class BloomFilter:
    def __init__(self, n: int, fp_rate: float):
        self.m = math.ceil(-n * math.log(fp_rate) / math.log(2) ** 2)
        self.k = max(1, round(self.m / n * math.log(2)))
        self.bits = bytearray((self.m + 7) // 8)

    def _positions(self, item: str):
        d = hashlib.sha256(item.encode()).digest()
        h1 = int.from_bytes(d[:8], "big")
        h2 = int.from_bytes(d[8:16], "big") | 1
        return [(h1 + i * h2) % self.m for i in range(self.k)]

    def add(self, item: str):
        for pos in self._positions(item):
            self.bits[pos // 8] |= 1 << (pos % 8)

    def __contains__(self, item: str) -> bool:
        return all(self.bits[pos // 8] & (1 << (pos % 8)) for pos in self._positions(item))
  • Sizing: m = -n ln p / (ln 2)^2 bits and k = (m/n) ln 2 hashes. For 1B URLs at 1% false positives that is ~9.6 bits per item, ~1.2 GB, with 7 hashes.
  • No false negatives; false positives mean we skip a few unseen URLs, acceptable for a crawler.
  • Double hashing (h1 + i x h2) derives k positions from one hash.
  • No deletes (use a counting Bloom filter) and it cannot grow past n without the false positive rate rising (use scalable Bloom filters or rebuild).

Complexity: O(k) per add and lookup, m bits of memory regardless of item size.
fields.Hint: k hash positions into an m bit array.
fields.Fact: Bloom filters trade a tunable false positive rate for tiny memory and no false negatives.
fields.Source:
Space/Time Trade-offs in Hash Coding with Allowable Errors (https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/362686.362692)
System Design Interview: An Insider's Guide, Volume 1 (https://bytebytego.com/)

fields.Question: Design collaborative document editing like Google Docs, where many users type in the same document at once and see each other's changes live.
fields.Answer:
• Connection: each client keeps a WebSocket to the document's session server; all editors of one document are routed to the same server (consistent hashing on doc_id).
  • Concurrency control: clients apply edits locally for instant feedback, send operations with the version they were based on. The server orders operations and transforms concurrent ones (Operational Transformation), or the system uses CRDTs where operations commute and merge without a central transform.
  • Persistence: append operations to a log per document; periodically snapshot the full document so loading does not replay everything. Version history comes from the log.
  • Presence: cursors and selections broadcast as ephemeral messages, not persisted.
  • Offline: queue local operations, rebase or merge on reconnect (CRDTs make this simpler).

Tradeoffs: OT needs a central server per document but keeps payloads small; CRDTs allow peer to peer and offline but carry metadata overhead. Mention that a single session server per document bounds concurrency per doc, which is fine for human editing.
fields.Hint: Ordered operation log per document with OT or CRDT merging.
fields.Fact: Live co editing is local first edits plus a convergent merge of concurrent operations.
fields.Source:
Designing Data-Intensive Applications (https://dataintensive.net/)
RFC 6455: The WebSocket Protocol (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6455)

fields.Question: The interviewer asks: "How would you make this service survive the loss of an entire region?" Walk through the options.
fields.Answer:
• Active passive: one region serves, data replicates async to a standby. Simple; failover loses the replication lag worth of writes (RPO) and takes minutes (RTO) to promote and shift DNS.
  • Active active with partitioned ownership: each user or tenant has a home region for writes; reads anywhere. No write conflicts; a region loss needs re homing users.
  • Active active multi leader: writes anywhere, async replication, conflict resolution (last write wins, CRDTs). Lowest latency, hardest correctness.
  • Globally consistent DB (Spanner, CockroachDB): consensus across regions; strong consistency, but every write pays cross region latency (tens to 100+ ms).

Also: global load balancing (GeoDNS or anycast) with health checks, stateless services deployed in every region, capacity to absorb a failed region's traffic (N+1), and regular failover drills. State the RPO and RTO you are targeting and pick the cheapest option that meets them.
fields.Hint: Pick from RPO and RTO: active passive, partitioned active active, or consensus.
fields.Fact: Multi region design is a choice of how much consistency and latency you trade for surviving a region loss.
fields.Source:
Designing Data-Intensive Applications (https://dataintensive.net/)
Spanner: Google's Globally Distributed Database (https://research.google/pubs/spanner-googles-globally-distributed-database-2/)
Consistency Tradeoffs in Modern Distributed Database System Design (https://www.cs.umd.edu/~abadi/papers/abadi-pacelc.pdf)

fields.Question: Your feed API uses ?page=500&size=20 and gets slower and shows duplicates as new posts arrive. How do you redesign pagination?
fields.Answer:
• Offset problem: OFFSET 10000 makes the DB scan and discard 10,000 rows; inserts at the head shift pages so users see duplicates or miss items.
  • Cursor (keyset) pagination: return an opaque cursor encoding the last item's sort key, for example (created_at, id). Next page: WHERE (created_at, id) < (?, ?) ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 20. Uses the index, O(page size), stable under inserts.
  • Include the unique id as a tiebreaker so items with equal timestamps are not skipped.
  • Encode the cursor (base64 of JSON, optionally signed) so clients cannot depend on its format.

Tradeoff: cursors cannot jump to page 500 directly; offer search or date filters instead. For ranked feeds, snapshot the ranked list for the session and paginate over the snapshot.
fields.Hint: Keyset cursor on (sort key, id).
fields.Fact: Cursor pagination is constant cost per page and stable while data changes.
fields.Source:
Designing Data-Intensive Applications (https://dataintensive.net/)
RFC 9110: HTTP Semantics (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110)

fields.Question: Design a nearby places service like Yelp: given a location and radius, return the top rated businesses nearby. 200M businesses, read heavy, businesses rarely change.
fields.Answer:
• Read heavy and static: precompute a geospatial index and replicate it widely; updates can propagate within minutes.
  • Index: geohash (or quadtree, since data is static and density varies a lot between cities and countryside). Store geohash_prefix -> business_ids. Query the cell for the radius plus neighbors, filter by exact distance, rank by rating and distance.
  • Storage: business details in a sharded DB with a cache; the geo index in memory on read replicas (200M x ~30 bytes of id plus coordinates is ~6 GB, fits in memory).
  • Pick cell size from radius: use a coarser geohash precision for larger radii so you query a handful of cells.
  • Scaling: replicate the read only index; shard business details by business id.

Contrast with ride sharing: there points move every few seconds, so you favor fixed cells and in memory updates; here points are static, so a density adaptive quadtree or a DB geo index (PostGIS) is fine.
fields.Hint: Static geo index replicated in memory, cell plus neighbors.
fields.Fact: When points are static, precompute and replicate the spatial index; move complexity off the write path.
fields.Source:
System Design Interview: An Insider's Guide, Volume 2 (https://bytebytego.com/)
Redis: Geospatial indexes (https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/data-types/geospatial/)
